title: Long noncoding RNA Malat1 protects against osteoporosis and bone metastasis

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The authors state that "across the four patient groups, MALAT1 expression levels in pre-osteoclasts and osteoclasts were significantly lower in patients with osteoporosis, osteosarcoma, or breast cancer bone metastasis than in the non-osteoporotic individual (Fig. 4i–k)". The control group consists of a single individual (GSE169396: "a non-osteoporotic individual and three osteoporosis patients"). A claim of statistical significance against an n = 1 control can only be obtained by treating individual cells as independent replicates (pseudoreplication); there is no biological replication in the reference group, so the reported significance is not interpretable.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results, single-cell RNA-seq analysis (GSE190772, GSE162454, GSE169396 comparison)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: MALAT1 expression levels are compared quantitatively between cells taken from three entirely different GEO datasets (different patients, tissues, sample-processing and sequencing batches). Harmony, which the authors used, corrects the low-dimensional embedding for clustering/annotation; it does not produce batch-corrected expression values suitable for cross-dataset quantitative comparison. MALAT1 in particular is extremely sensitive to nuclear content, dissociation protocol and ambient RNA, so the between-dataset difference is confounded with batch and cannot support the stated conclusion.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract ("single-cell transcriptome analysis of clinical bone samples reveals that reduced MALAT1 expression ... is associated with osteoporosis and metastatic bone lesions") and end of Fig. 4 section
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The stated association rests on a comparison with one non-osteoporotic control individual and on cross-dataset expression comparisons; the data cannot establish a disease association. The wording ("reveals", "indicate that reduced MALAT1 expression in the osteoclast lineage is associated with osteoporosis") overstates what an n = 1 control, batch-confounded analysis can show. In addition, osteosarcoma (a primary bone tumour) is folded into "metastatic bone lesions" in the abstract.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results: EO771 description ("a cell line derived from a mouse mammary tumor on a C57BL/6 background³⁸") vs. single-cell section ("GSE190772 with samples from two patients with breast cancer bone metastases³⁸,⁴³")
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Reference 38 is cited both as the source describing the mouse EO771 mammary tumour cell line and as a source for a human breast-cancer bone-metastasis single-cell dataset (GSE190772). The same reference cannot plausibly support both claims; at least one citation is misattributed.

predicted_errors.error_location: Results, first paragraph on MGCs: "human placental CD14⁺ macrophages into MGCs²⁹ (Fig. 1a), in which osteoclasts are the major cell population⁸"
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Multinucleated giant cells formed from placental (Hofbauer-type) CD14⁺ macrophages are not osteoclasts, and reference 8 (a general osteoclast biology citation) cannot establish that osteoclasts are the "major cell population" of such cultures. This unsupported assertion is what licenses the authors to treat a non-bone, non-RANKL-driven MGC dataset as a model of osteoclastogenesis, so it materially affects the interpretation of Fig. 1a–d.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract ("Malat1 deficiency in mice promotes osteoporosis and bone metastasis of melanoma and mammary tumor cells") vs. Results (intratibial injection of B16F1 and EO771)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Both tumour experiments used direct intratibial injection, which assays bone colonization/outgrowth, not metastatic dissemination. The Results themselves use the more accurate phrase "metastatic bone colonization", but the abstract and the title-level claim present the data as demonstrating protection against "bone metastasis", overstating the model's scope.

The legend states "Statistical significance in c, e–h, and j–m was determined by a two-tailed unpaired t test", yet panels j–m contain four treatment conditions (untreated, RANKL, LPS/TNF-α with and without RANKL priming), so multiple pairwise t tests are performed without any multiple-comparison correction (ANOVA/post hoc testing required). Moreover, panel c reports uncorrected t tests on the same RNA-seq data for which panel b explicitly used a linear model with Benjamini–Hochberg correction, an internally inconsistent statistical treatment of one dataset.
